title: Antidepressant Discontinuation Syndrome - Withdrawal Management
scenario: Sarah Mitchell, a 34-year-old marketing manager, presents to your GP clinic with distressing symptoms after stopping her venlafaxine 150mg daily abruptly 5 days ago. She had been taking the medication for 18 months for major depression but decided to stop because she felt well and was concerned about weight gain. She now reports electric shock sensations in her head, dizziness when turning her head, nausea, vivid dreams, and feeling emotionally labile with crying spells. She is worried these symptoms mean her depression is returning and feels frustrated that she wasn't warned about withdrawal effects.

patient_demographics.relevant_history: Major depressive disorder diagnosed 18 months ago, responded well to venlafaxine, no previous suicide attempts, no substance use, family history of depression (mother)

initial_vital_signs.other: Mild diaphoresis, no tremor, pupils equal and reactive

expected_actions: Recognise antidepressant discontinuation syndrome from abrupt SNRI cessation
Differentiate from depression relapse through symptom timing and characteristics
Explain brain zaps and sensory disturbances as withdrawal phenomena
Assess current mood and suicide risk using SAFE-T protocol
Restart venlafaxine at previous dose to relieve symptoms
Develop gradual tapering schedule over 4-8 weeks minimum
Educate about SNRI withdrawal timeline and symptom management
Consider switching to fluoxetine for easier discontinuation if appropriate
Schedule regular follow-up during taper period
Document withdrawal symptoms and management plan
expected_investigations: Mental state examination focusing on mood and anxiety symptoms
PHQ-9 score to assess current depression severity
Review medication adherence history
Consider UEC if severe nausea/vomiting
No routine blood tests required for discontinuation syndrome
expected_management: Immediate: Restart venlafaxine 75mg BD (or previous dose) to abort withdrawal
Symptom relief expected within 24-48 hours of restarting
Gradual taper plan: Reduce by 37.5mg every 2 weeks
Final taper: 37.5mg daily → 37.5mg alternate days → stop
Alternative: Switch to fluoxetine 20mg for 1 week then stop
Supportive measures: Regular exercise, sleep hygiene, stress management
Patient education about withdrawal vs relapse
Written taper schedule provided
Safety net advice for severe symptoms
Consider psychological support during discontinuation

criteria: Timeline of medication cessation clearly established
Specific withdrawal symptoms documented (brain zaps, dizziness)
Previous antidepressant response and duration explored
Current mood and functional status assessed

equipment_needed: Patient information leaflet on antidepressant withdrawal
station_setup.actor_instructions: Present as distressed about physical symptoms, particularly the 'electric shock' sensations. Express frustration about not being warned about withdrawal. Show relief when symptoms are validated as withdrawal rather than relapse.

red_flags: Signs of serotonin syndrome if other serotonergic drugs involved
common_pitfalls: Misdiagnosing as depression relapse without considering timeline

australian_context.pbs_medications: Venlafaxine PBS code 8523H (150mg), Fluoxetine PBS code 2089L (20mg)
australian_context.local_guidelines: RANZCP guidelines recommend minimum 4-week taper for SNRIs
australian_context.referral_pathways: GP management usually sufficient, psychiatrist if complex polypharmacy
australian_context.medicare_billing: MBS Item 23 (Level B consultation) or 36 (Mental health consultation)

title: Body Dysmorphic Disorder - SSRI and CBT
scenario: James Chen, a 22-year-old university student, is brought to your clinic by his concerned mother. He has been increasingly isolating himself, missing classes, and spending 4-5 hours daily examining and trying to hide what he perceives as a severely asymmetrical nose. He has taken over 1000 selfies in the past month, constantly checking his appearance, and has consulted three plastic surgeons who all stated his nose appears normal. He avoids social situations, covers mirrors at home, and has dropped out of his engineering course. His mother reports he seems depressed and has mentioned feeling hopeless about his appearance. He reluctantly admits to checking his reflection in windows and phone screens dozens of times daily.

patient_demographics.relevant_history: No previous psychiatric treatment, perfectionist personality, high academic achiever before symptom onset 8 months ago, no substance use, family history of OCD (sister)

initial_vital_signs.other: Well-groomed but wearing cap pulled low, avoiding eye contact

expected_actions: Assess body dysmorphic disorder using DSM-5 criteria
Screen for depression and suicidality (BDD has high suicide risk)
Evaluate insight level and readiness for treatment
Explore specific behaviours (mirror checking, camouflaging, reassurance seeking)
Document functional impairment in academic and social domains
Initiate SSRI at higher doses (fluoxetine 60-80mg or sertraline 200mg)
Refer for specialised CBT for BDD (exposure and response prevention)
Educate about BDD as treatable psychiatric condition
Involve family in psychoeducation with consent
Establish therapeutic alliance despite poor insight
expected_investigations: Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale Modified for BDD (BDD-YBOCS)
PHQ-9 for comorbid depression screening
GAD-7 for anxiety assessment
Comprehensive mental state examination
No physical investigations unless medical differentials suspected
expected_diagnosis: Body Dysmorphic Disorder with absent insight, secondary major depression
expected_management: Pharmacotherapy: Start fluoxetine 20mg daily, increase by 20mg weekly to 60-80mg
Higher SSRI doses required than for depression alone
Alternative: Sertraline up to 200mg daily if fluoxetine ineffective
CBT for BDD: 16-20 sessions including exposure and response prevention
Exposure tasks: Gradual reduction in checking and camouflaging behaviours
Response prevention: Resist mirror checking, seeking reassurance
Perceptual retraining exercises
Family psychoeducation about not providing reassurance
Regular monitoring for suicidal ideation
Consider clomipramine if SSRI fails (requires ECG monitoring)

criteria: Suicide risk evaluated given high-risk condition
Mental state examination with focus on insight
Correct BDD diagnosis using DSM-5 criteria

station_setup.actor_instructions: Initially reluctant to discuss concerns, frequently touch or adjust cap/hat. Show poor insight - insist the defect is real and visible to everyone. Become slightly more engaged when doctor validates distress without agreeing with perception.

red_flags: Active suicidal ideation (BDD has suicide rate 45x general population)
Psychotic features (may indicate delusional disorder instead)
Multiple cosmetic procedures planned or undertaken
common_pitfalls: Using standard SSRI doses instead of high doses required for BDD
Referring to plastic surgery without treating BDD
Missing high suicide risk in BDD

australian_context.pbs_medications: Fluoxetine PBS code 2089L (20mg), requires authority for 60-80mg doses
australian_context.local_guidelines: RANZCP recommends specialist CBT for BDD when available
australian_context.referral_pathways: Better Access scheme for psychology (up to 10 sessions initially)
australian_context.medicare_billing: MBS Item 291 (Psychiatrist initial consultation), Item 80110 (Psychology CBT)

title: Trichotillomania - Habit Reversal Training

She tearfully reveals she has been pulling out her hair since age 12, with worsening during exam periods. She has multiple bald patches on her scalp and has also been pulling her eyebrows and eyelashes. She describes an increasing tension before pulling and relief afterwards, often doing it while studying or watching TV without full awareness. She has tried wearing gloves and cutting her hair short but continues to pull. She is distressed about starting clinical placements next year and fears her appearance will affect her professional image. She denies eating the hair but admits to playing with and examining the pulled strands.

patient_demographics.relevant_history: Onset age 12 during parents' divorce, perfectionist traits, mild social anxiety, no previous treatment for trichotillomania, tried self-help strategies unsuccessfully

initial_vital_signs.other: Visible alopecia patches on scalp, thinned eyebrows, some missing eyelashes

expected_actions: Assess trichotillomania severity and functional impact
Screen for body-focused repetitive behaviours (skin picking, nail biting)
Evaluate for trichophagia (eating hair) and risk of trichobezoar
Explore triggers and high-risk situations (studying, stress, boredom)
Assess awareness levels (automatic vs focused pulling)
Explain habit reversal training components
Teach competing response (clenching fists when urge arises)
Implement stimulus control strategies
Consider N-acetylcysteine supplementation (1200-2400mg daily)
Discuss SSRI if severe or with comorbid anxiety/depression
expected_investigations: Massachusetts General Hospital Hairpulling Scale
Screen for anxiety and depression (GAD-7, PHQ-9)
Dermatological examination to exclude alopecia areata
Consider iron studies and thyroid function if indicated
No routine investigations specifically for trichotillomania
expected_management: Habit Reversal Training (HRT): Primary treatment modality
Awareness training: Self-monitoring diary, identify triggers
Competing response: Clench fists for 1 minute when urge occurs
Stimulus control: Barriers to pulling (gloves, bandaids on fingers)
Modify environment: Cover mirrors, improve lighting while studying
N-acetylcysteine 600mg BD, increase to 1200mg BD after 4 weeks
Consider clomipramine 25mg nocte if HRT insufficient (requires ECG)
Stress management: Mindfulness, progressive muscle relaxation
Support group referral or online resources (TLC Foundation)
Regular follow-up to monitor progress and adjust strategies

station_setup.actor_instructions: Initially embarrassed and reluctant to remove headscarf. Demonstrate subtle hair touching/twirling during consultation. Show relief when doctor is non-judgmental. Express motivation for treatment due to career concerns.

Delusional beliefs about hair (may indicate other disorder)
Complete social isolation due to appearance
common_pitfalls: Focusing only on medication without behavioural intervention

australian_context.local_guidelines: No specific Australian guidelines, international consensus favours HRT
australian_context.referral_pathways: Better Access for psychology (10 sessions), dermatology if diagnostic doubt

title: Hoarding Disorder - Motivational Interviewing
scenario: Robert Patterson, a 68-year-old retired librarian, is brought to your clinic by his adult daughter who is extremely concerned about his living conditions. She reports that his house has become increasingly cluttered over the past 5 years since his wife died, with newspapers, books, and miscellaneous items filling most rooms. She describes narrow pathways through the clutter, blocked exits, and inability to use the kitchen properly. The local council has issued a notice requiring cleanup within 30 days or facing eviction. Robert minimises the problem, stating the items have sentimental value and might be useful someday. He becomes agitated when discussing disposal of items and has refused previous attempts to help clear the house.

patient_demographics.relevant_history: Wife died 5 years ago, gradual accumulation since, mild depression treated with sertraline 50mg, no cognitive impairment on recent GP review, socially isolated

initial_vital_signs.other: Unkempt appearance, clothes appear worn and not recently washed

expected_actions: Assess hoarding severity using Clutter Image Rating Scale
Evaluate safety risks (fire hazards, falls, hygiene issues)
Screen for cognitive impairment with MMSE or MoCA
Use motivational interviewing to explore ambivalence
Identify personal values and link to behaviour change
Assess decision-making capacity regarding living situation
Explore grief and connection to accumulation behaviour
Develop harm reduction approach rather than forced clearing
Engage family while respecting autonomy
Consider home visit for accurate assessment
expected_investigations: Clutter Image Rating Scale (patient and family ratings)
Saving Inventory-Revised (SI-R) questionnaire
Cognitive screening (MMSE or MoCA)
Activities of Daily Living (ADL) assessment
Home environment assessment if possible
Depression and anxiety screening
expected_diagnosis: Hoarding Disorder, severe, with poor insight; Complicated grief
expected_management: Motivational interviewing approach: Explore ambivalence non-judgmentally
Values clarification: What matters most? (family relationships, independence)
Harm reduction: Start with safety issues only (clear exits, remove fire hazards)
Graduated approach: Sort items into keep/donate/discard with support
CBT for hoarding: Challenge beliefs about possessions, reduce acquiring
Increase sertraline to 100-150mg for hoarding symptoms
Grief counselling for unresolved bereavement
Family therapy to improve communication and reduce conflict
Liaison with council for extension or graduated compliance
Professional organiser specialising in hoarding if available

station_setup.actor_instructions: Initially defensive about possessions, soften when doctor shows understanding rather than judgment. Express fear of losing memories of deceased wife. Show ambivalence - acknowledge some concern but resist immediate action.
props: Small collection of items (newspapers, books) patient brought

red_flags: Immediate safety risks (blocked exits, fire hazards)
common_pitfalls: Not assessing capacity and assuming incompetence

australian_context.local_guidelines: No specific Australian hoarding guidelines; follow international CBT protocols
australian_context.referral_pathways: Aged Care Assessment Team (ACAT), council social services, specialist hoarding services in major cities
australian_context.medicare_billing: MBS Item 23 (Level B), Item 2713 (Mental health plan), Item 10997 (Home visit if required)

title: Gender Dysphoria - Referral and Hormone Therapy

He has been binding his chest daily, sometimes for over 12 hours, and has experienced some rib pain. He has strong family support and has been seeing a psychologist for 6 months who has written a support letter. He is seeking testosterone therapy and eventual top surgery.

Pregnancy test before starting testosterone
Consider pelvic ultrasound if menstrual irregularities

title: Autism Spectrum Disorder in Adults - Diagnosis and Support
scenario: Jessica Wong, a 32-year-old software developer, presents after her 8-year-old son was recently diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. She describes lifelong difficulties with social interactions, taking things literally, and becoming overwhelmed in busy environments. She has maintained employment through strict routines and working remotely. She masks her difficulties by rehearsing conversations and copying others' social behaviours, leading to exhaustion. She has few friendships, experiences sensory sensitivities (tags in clothes, certain textures), and has intense interests in coding and Japanese animation. She wonders if this explains her lifelong feeling of being different.
